pride_data.title: An Intrinsically Disordered Region of Ubp10 Governs its Specificity for Deubiquitinating H2A/H2B Dimers over Nucleosomes
pride_data.projectDescription: Histone modifications perform a vast array of functions in regulating gene expression, DNA replication, and repair. Monoubiquitination of histone H2B at K123 in yeast (K120 in humans) is an intriguing modification because it is deposited cotranscriptionally, mediates the installation of several other epigenetic marks, and then disappears; hence, it is associated transiently with actively transcribed chromatin. In yeast, the H2B ubiquitin writer is the E2/E3 pair Rad6/Bre1, and there are two deubiquitinases that can erase it, Ubp8 and Ubp10. Whilst Ubp8 resides within the larger SAGA complex, Ubp10 (USP36 in humans) is a monomeric and constitutively active deubiquitinase, raising questions as to what processes regulate it, given it would be undesirable for H2B to be deubiquitinated prematurely before downstream processes connected to this epigenetic mark occur. Here we show that Ubp10’s activity is regulated by acidic regions within its long N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which extensively interact with H2A/H2B dimers, as shown by crosslinking mass spectrometry. These interactions vanish when H2A/H2B is present in nucleosomes. These observations explain why Ubp10 has low baseline activity on nucleosomes, but is activated by FACT, a histone chaperone which evicts H2A/H2B dimers from nucleosomes, thereby generating Ubp10’s preferred substrate, which we demonstrate with single molecule fluorescence experiments. Hence, this work provides a biophysical mechanism for how Ubp10 can provide a housekeeping function to deubiquitinate actively-transcribed DNA, wherein FACT produces a temporary pool of H2A/H2B dimers.
pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: Chemical crosslinking of Ubp10 with the H2A/H2B dimers and nucleosomes. H2A/H2B-flag, H2A/H2B-Ub, NCP-flag, and NCP-Ub were each crosslinked with Ubp10 using DSBU or EDC. To make the 50 µl reactions, 10 mM Ubp10 was mixed with 10 mM H2A/H2B-flag, 10 mM H2A/H2B-Ub, 5 mM NCP-flag or 5 mM NCP-Ub in DSBU reaction buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP) or EDC reaction buffer (20 mM MES pH 6.0, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP). Samples were incubated on ice for one hour to allow for complex formation.   To crosslink the samples with DSBU, a freshly prepared stock of 50 mM DSBU in anhydrous DMSO (1 µL) was added to each DSBU reaction mixture to achieve a crosslinker concentration of 1 mM. Samples were gently mixed and incubated on an end-over-end rotator for 45 mins at 10 rpm at room temperature. The reaction was quenched with the addition of 100 mM Tris at pH 8 and incubated for five minutes at room temperature. Finally, DTT was added to a concentration of 20 mM.   To crosslink the samples with EDC, a freshly prepared stock of 0.5 M EDC, 0.25 M sulfo-NHS (1 µL) was added to each EDC reaction mixture so that the final concentration of the crosslinker was 10 mM. Samples were gently mixed and incubated on an end-over-end rotator for two hours at 10 rpm at room temperature. The reaction was quenched with 20 mM DTT.   Sample preparation for cross-linking mass spectrometry. Solid urea (48.05 mg) was added to each crosslinked sample. Samples were diluted to a volume of 100 µl with 20 mM HEPES at pH 8 to achieve a urea concentration of 8 M and a DTT concentration of 10 mM. Samples were incubated on a thermoblock at 37oC for 45 minutes at 700 rpm to reduce disulfide bonds. Cysteine residues were alkylated with 40 mM IAA in the dark for 30 minutes at room temperature. Samples were diluted with an addition of 300 µl of 20 mM Tris at pH 8 to achieve a urea concentration to 2M. For the primary digest, trypsin was added to each sample at a 1:50 enzyme to substrate mass ratio and digested on a thermoblock overnight at 25oC, 700 rpm.    Samples were divided into equal volumes and half of each sample was processed by a serial digest with Glu-C. For the serial digest, each sample was diluted with 20 mM Tris at pH 8 to a final urea concentration of 0.8 M. Glu-C was added to each sample at a 1:50 enzyme to substrate mass ratio, and samples were digested overnight on a thermoblock at 30oC, 700 rpm.    Single and serially digested samples were acidified with the addition of 0.5% TFA. Desalting was performed with Waters Sep-Pak C18 solid phase extraction cartridges. Cartridges were loaded onto a vacuum manifold and conditioned twice with 1.0 ml 80% ACN, 0.5% TFA in Optima water, then equilibrated four times with 1.0 ml 0.5% TFA in Optima water. Acidified samples were slowly loaded onto the cartridges under a diminished vacuum. The cartridges were washed four times with 1.0 ml 0.5% TFA in Optima water. Cartridges were placed over 15 ml conical tubes, and peptides were eluted using 1.0 ml 80% ACN, 0.5% TFA in Optima water and centrifuging (Eppendorf 5910R) at 350 rpm for 5 minutes. Eluted peptides were transferred to microfuge tubes and dried in a vacuum centrifuge (Eppendorf Vacufuge). Dried samples were stored at -80ºC. Before analysis, the peptides were vigorously resuspended in 0.1% FA in Optima water to a final concentration of 1 mg/ml. Mass spectrometry data acquisition. Samples were analyzed in technical duplicate by LC-MS/MS on an UltiMate3000 UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled with a Q-Exactive HF-X Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides accumulated on a precolumn C18 trap cartridge (Acclaim PepMap 100, C18, 75 µm x 2 cm, 3µm, 100 Å column) and resolved on an Acclaim PepMap RSLC, C18, 75 µm x 25 cm, 2µm, 100 Å column (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Solvent A, consisted of 0.1% FA in 2% ACN, 98% water, and solvent B, consisted of 0.1% FA in ACN. Approximately 1 µg of peptides were injected onto the column for each run. After washing the trap cartridge with solvent A for 10 minutes, the trap cartridge was switched to be in-line with the separating column.
pride_data.dataProcessingProtocol: Mass spectrometry data analysis and cross-link identification. Raw XL-MS data were converted to the mzML file format and centroided using the MsConvert GUI from the ProteoWizard Toolkit version 3 ​(69)​. Crosslinks were identified using MeroX version 2.0.1.4 ​(52)​. For tryptic digests, protease sites were defined after arginine and lysine residues, with lysine blocked by proline as a cleavage site. For serial digests, protease sites were allowed at arginine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, and lysine with lysine blocked by proline as a cleavage site. For both single and serial digests, a maximum of three missed cleavages were allowed, the minimum peptide length was set to 3, and the maximum peptide length was set to 30. Oxidation of methionine was defined as a variable modification (maximum of one variable modification allowed per peptide), and cysteine carbamidomethylation was defined as a static modification.    The default MeroX settings were used to define the crosslinking parameters for DSBU and EDC. Precursor precision was set to 5 ppm, fragment ion precision was set to 10 ppm, the mass range was set to 200.0-6000.0 Da, the signal-to-noise ratio was set to 2.0, b and y ions were selected, the minimum number of fragments per peptide was set to 3, the minimum charge was set to 2, and deisotoping mode was selected. For each sample, the appropriate mass recalibrations at both the MS1 and MS2 levels were determined by searching for linear peptides in Proteome Discoverer version 2.4 and plotting the Δm. Searches were conducted in quadratic mode using FASTA files containing the appropriate proteins for each sample. The FDR cutoff was set to 1%, and all scores above the FDR cutoff were accepted. Data visualizations were prepared using crosslink data files exported from MeroX and uploaded to the xVis and XiView websites ​(70, 71)​.
